The Committee's view of inflation worsened between 2021 and 2022. Inflation remained elevated throughout, with core PCE inflation rising from 4.6% in July 2021 to 5.1% in September 2022 [2022-11-02/staffEconomy/3]. The Committee expressed concern that high inflation could raise public expectations, making it harder to achieve its longer-run inflation target [2021-12-15/participantsViews/9]. Market expectations also rose, from 2.16% in Q3 2022 to 2.27% in December 2022, reflecting growing concern about persistent inflation.

The Committee's view of the labor market worsened between 2008 and 2009. In December 2008, it noted rapid job losses across industries and declining hiring plans [2008-12-16/staffEconomy/2]. By June 2009, participants still saw substantial job losses and a rapidly rising unemployment rate [2009-06-24/participantsViews/6]. The unemployment rate rose from 6.8% in 2008 to 10% in November 2009, and nonfarm payrolls declined year-over-year by 3.5% [2009-11-01]. Weekly jobless claims also increased from 533,000 in 2008 to 468,000 in December 2009, indicating persistent labor market weakness.

Between 2019 and 2020, the Committee's view shifted from acknowledging weak investment and exports to emphasizing that the pandemic posed significant downside risks to the economy. In 2019, the Committee noted weak investment and exports and removed "act as appropriate" language, signaling a more structured outlook. By 2020, the staff viewed risks as tilted to the downside, with a heightened probability of a pandemic resurgence [2020-11-05/staffOutlook/3]. The economic outlook became more pessimistic, with inflation and growth revised lower in staff forecasts, and real consumer spending growth slowing to -2.4% [2020-11-05/staffOutlook/1]. The Committee's view of interest rate policy evolved from a cautious stance in 2015 to a more hawkish one by 2018. Between 2015 and 2018, the federal funds rate target increased from 0 to 1/4 percent to 2-1/4 to 2-1/2 percent, with 9 increases, 0 cuts, and 23 holds across 31 meetings [2015-12-16/policyAction/5]. Dissenting votes were present, with 4 for lower rates and 8 for higher rates, reflecting growing confidence in a tighter policy [2017-12-13/policyAction/15; 2016-11-02/policyAction/17]. The Committee consistently emphasized maintaining moderate inflation and labor market strength, with no major shifts in direction.
